property_summary: For any nonzero ETH deposit sent to C via receive, the depositsCount stored in C strictly increases by 1 after the call; the mutant incorrectly reverts when depositsCount is at its max uint (making some valid deposits fail).
For every successful payable receive call, C.depositsCount increases by exactly 1 (the mutant reverts when depositsCount is at uint256 max, breaking this rule for some input).

For any successful external payable transfer into C (via receive), C.depositsCount never decreases and always increases by exactly 1; the mutant that changes the require to '>' will revert when depositsCount is max uint, violating that the receive remains callable for those inputs.

For any caller and any value, a successful payable call to receive() always returns (does not revert) when depositsCount is any uint < type(uint).max, but the mutant reverts for the special input where depositsCount == uint.max and a nonzero deposit is sent, so the reference accepts that call while the mutant rejects it.

For any deposit value and caller, the reference contract always accepts a 0-value payable call to receive() (never reverts) and increments depositsCount by 1; the mutant (which requires depositsCount+1 > depositsCount) will revert when depositsCount is already max uint256 even for a 0-value call, breaking this universal property.

Every successful payable call to receive() on the correct contract increments depositsCount by at most 1 per call (i.e., depositsCount after the call equals prior + 1 and never overflows), whereas the mutant unconditionally increments allowing sequences of calls that can make depositsCount larger than allowed when callers revert or when overflow concerns arise; we test that a single payable receive() call increases depositsCount exactly by 1 for any sender and amount.

For any caller and any payable amount, if the caller's receive() invocation executes (does not revert), the reference contract increments depositsCount by exactly 1 per successful call even if the callee (an external counterparty) reverts during a subsequent external call; the mutant increments unconditionally so a failing external call can cause an extra increment to be observable via depositsCount.

For any payable call to C.receive() that is invoked (does not revert), the reference increments depositsCount by exactly 1; the mutant increments unconditionally even when an external low-level call from receive would revert, so some inputs (a reverting callee) produce a discrepancy.

For any payable call that reaches C.receive(), depositsCount increases by exactly 1; the mutant that removes the require can make depositsCount increase even when a nested external call fails, so some inputs (a failing callee) produce a differing depositsCount.

For any Ether payment to C via receive(), depositsCount will never wrap-around (i.e., incrementing from the old value yields a value >= old value); the mutant removing the require can allow an overflow/wrap so depositsCount < previous value for some fuzzed initial depositsCount and payment sequence.

For any caller sending a positive ether value to the contract's receive() (so the call succeeds), the reference contract increments depositsCount by 1 (so depositsCount increases after the call); the mutant that unconditionally reverts breaks this by making the receive always revert and thus depositsCount does not increase / the call fails.

For any sender sending nonzero ether to C via its receive, the reference contract accepts the transfer and increments depositsCount (call succeeds), whereas the mutant always reverts causing the receive call to fail for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonzero ether amount sent to C via its receive, the reference contract accepts the payment (the low-level call succeeds) while the mutant that reverts in receive causes the receive call to fail for some inputs (some amount/sender), so assert that the receive call succeeds (ok == true).

For every EOA sender and any nonzero ether amount, calling C's receive() succeeds (does not revert) and thus the low-level call returns/does not revert; the mutant that unconditionally reverts in receive() will cause such a funded call to fail for some inputs, so the property is that funded receive() calls from EOAs always succeed.

For any caller and any nonzero ETH amount sent to C via its receive(), the reference contract accepts the payment and increases depositsCount (so a funded low-level send to C succeeds and leaves depositsCount > 0 for that caller/amount), whereas the mutant that unconditionally reverts inside receive() will cause such funded calls to fail (revert) for some inputs, violating that receiving funded transfers succeeds and updates depositsCount.

On any successful receive() call that sends >0 wei to the contract, the reference increments depositsCount by 1 (so depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before), whereas the mutant decrements it, violating that non-decreasing property for some input amounts.

For any successful payable call to receive, depositsCount never decreases (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant decrements depositsCount on receive, breaking this non-decreasing property for some inputs.

For any single successful payable call to receive(), depositsCount increases by exactly 1 (i.e., depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1); the mutant decrements instead, so for some input the equality fails.

For any initial depositsCount and any sequence where a non-owner address sends ETH via the contract's receive (i.e., payable transfer to the contract), depositsCount only changes when the sender is the contract owner — in the reference receive increments depositsCount regardless of sender (so depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before), while the mutant decrements causing depositsCount_after < depositsCount_before for some inputs; we instead assert that making the contract receive a zero-value payment does not change depositsCount (reference: unchanged; mutant: decrements and thus violates).

For any sender and any value, after calling the contract's receive() (a payable plain transfer), the depositsCount is never decreased (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant that decrements depositsCount on receive violates this for some inputs.

For every payable call to receive(), the reference contract never allows depositsCount to wrap-around (it is non-decreasing and thus depositsCount after a deposit is >= previous value), whereas the mutant using unchecked increment can overflow and make depositsCount smaller for some input amounts.

After any payable receive call, depositsCount never decreases (new value >= old value) in the reference; the mutant's unchecked increment can overflow so depositsCount can become smaller for some inputs, violating this non-decrease property.

For any single call to receive() the correct contract's depositsCount increases by exactly 1 (i.e. depositsCount_after == depositsCount_before + 1), whereas the mutant using unchecked increment can overflow and break this equality for some initial depositsCount values (when depositsCount == type(uint).max).

For any single payable receive call, the reference contract ensures depositsCount does not wrap-around (i.e., after a deposit depositsCount >= old value) even if the caller re-enters; the mutant's unchecked increment can overflow via a re-entrant sequence that increments depositsCount to uint256.max then triggers one more increment causing wrap-around, violating non-decrease.

For any single external payable call to receive(), the reference contract's depositsCount never decreases (depositsCount_after >= depositsCount_before); the mutant using unchecked can overflow on a carefully chosen starting depositsCount and one more increment making it wrap and thus decrease.
If this contract deposits some ether into C and then calls withdrawAll(), the caller's address (this) will gain all ether from C (address(this).balance increases by the withdrawn amount).
Calls to withdrawAll initiated by the contract owner must not revert (i.e., if the caller is the owner, withdrawAll succeeds).

For any recipient address and any contract balance, the reference contract's withdrawAll always results in contract balance being zero (all funds withdrawn via internal withdraw call), while the mutant that uses a direct transfer can fail to reduce the contract balance to zero when the recipient's fallback/receive reverts or otherwise causes transfer to revert; thus the reference preserves successful full withdrawal for all cases that the owner-initiated internal withdraw would have allowed, but the mutant can leave funds in the contract for some adversarial recipient behavior.

For any owner and any deposited amount, calling withdrawAll always sets the contract balance to zero on the reference (it forwards balance through its internal withdraw), but the mutant that uses a direct transfer can leave balance nonzero when the recipient reverts on receive/fallback.

For any owner, deposited amount, and adversarial recipient contract that reverts on receive/fallback, calling withdrawAll on the reference C always results in the contract balance being zero (the internal withdraw succeeds or forwards to withdraw which uses transfer to owner and does not observe the callee), whereas the mutant that replaces withdrawAll with a direct payable(msg.sender).transfer(address(this).balance) can revert or fail to withdraw when the recipient's receive/fallback reverts, leaving a non-zero contract balance.

For every owner and any deposited amount, calling withdrawAll on the reference C always results in the contract balance being zero (the internal withdraw call forwards funds via withdraw which uses transfer to msg.sender and is not affected by a malicious external callee), whereas the mutant that does a direct payable(msg.sender).transfer(address(this).balance) can fail when the owner's fallback/receive reverts (owner is a contract), leaving a non-zero contract balance — so the invariant is: after withdrawAll by the owner, address(c).balance == 0.

For any owner and any deposited amount, calling withdrawAll as the owner always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference implementation; the mutant's direct transfer to msg.sender can revert for some owner contract behaviors, so the mutant may cause withdrawAll to revert while the reference never does.
After depositing some ETH into c, calling withdrawAll by owner leaves c.balance == 0 (all funds forwarded to owner).
Calling withdraw(...) as the owner never reverts (succeeds) for any nonnegative value when msg.sender is the contract owner.
When the contract owner calls withdraw(...) the call never reverts (reverted == false) for any nonnegative _value that does not exceed the contract's balance.
withdraw should not revert when requested amount is <= contract balance

For any callee address and value, calling sendMoney on the correct contract never reverts when the callee's fallback/receive reverts (because transfer to the owner is not used there), but replacing transfer with call in withdraw can make sequences with a reentrant/failing callee change post-call balance behavior causing the property to be violated for some inputs.

After any sendMoney call from the contract to an arbitrary external callee, the contract's owner can always withdraw the same full contract balance (i.e., withdraw of address(c).balance succeeds); the mutant that replaces transfer with call can allow a callee to disrupt that (via reentrancy/failure) so withdraw may not succeed for some inputs.

For any recipient and amount, if the contract C receives ETH and then calls sendMoney(recipient, amount, data) where the recipient's fallback reverts, the reference C still allows the owner to withdraw the entire contract balance afterwards (withdraw(address(c).balance) succeeds); the mutant that switches transfer to call in withdraw can be broken by a reentrant or reverting recipient causing the owner withdraw to fail for some inputs.

For any nonzero deposit amount and any attacker fallback behavior, after the owner receives funds and the contract calls an external party via sendMoney, the reference contract always lets the owner successfully withdraw the contract's full balance using withdraw(address(c).balance); the mutant that replaces transfer with call can fail to deliver funds back to the owner for some attacker behaviors/inputs.

For any attacker address and any transfer amount, after sending ETH into C and invoking sendMoney(...) to that attacker, the legitimate owner can always withdraw the full contract balance using withdraw(address(c).balance); the mutant that replaces transfer with call in withdraw can be broken by a reentrant/attacking fallback so that withdraw(address(c).balance) fails for some inputs.
Only the original owner can reduce the contract balance via withdraw calls (so after a withdraw by a non-owner the contract balance stays >= prior balance).
